abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), encompassing Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, is characterized by chronic intestinal inflammation, epithelial barrier dysfunction, immune dysregulation, and aberrant extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling. Matrix metalloproteinase-2 (MMP-2), a zinc-dependent gelatinase, has emerged as a critical regulator of intestinal homeostasis owing to its dual role in tissue repair and inflammatory tissue destruction. Unlike several inducible matrix metalloproteinases, MMP-2 is constitutively expressed and tightly regulated through interactions with membrane-type MMPs, tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases (TIMPs), cytokines, redox signalling, and microbial factors. Dysregulated MMP-2 activity contributes to epithelial barrier disruption, leukocyte infiltration, chronic inflammation, fibrosis, and disease progression in IBD. This review summarizes the current understanding of MMP-2 biology, activation mechanisms, and immunopharmacological functions in intestinal inflammation, while critically evaluating therapeutic strategies aimed at its modulation. Particular emphasis is placed on natural and synthetic MMP-2 modulators, including animal-derived peptides and endogenous inhibitors, plant-derived polyphenols, flavonoids, alkaloids, terpenoids, and rationally designed small-molecule and peptidomimetic inhibitors. Emerging nanocarrier-based and targeted delivery systems are also discussed as approaches to enhance selectivity and minimize systemic toxicity. Furthermore, the review highlights the limitations of broad-spectrum MMP inhibition and underscores the need for site-specific modulation that preserves physiological tissue remodeling while suppressing pathological activity. Advances in precision medicine, single-cell and spatial transcriptomics, organoid-based disease models, and microbiome-informed therapeutic strategies are expected to facilitate the development of next-generation MMP-2-targeted interventions. Collectively, MMP-2 represents a promising yet complex therapeutic target whose successful modulation may improve long-term outcomes in IBD.
